Overview of Books I and II

The Islamic world is not a monolith. Islam as a religion cannot be equated with the Arab world as a political entity. There is an Iranian Islam, just as there is a Turkish, Indian, Indonesian, Malay, and other forms of Islam.

Unfortunately, readers who want to learn about Iran’s archaeology and art, both before and since Islam, can choose from a wealth of books. Far fewer books answer the question that confronts anyone seeking to understand the motives and inner life of Iranian consciousness—the forces that gave these outward forms their shape.

From the beginning, the Iranian world has formed a distinct whole within the Islamic community. Its particular character and calling become intelligible only when we consider Iran’s spiritual world as a continuous whole, before Islam and after its arrival. Islamic Iran has been, above all, the homeland of some of Islam’s greatest philosophers and mystics. For them, speculative thought can never be separated from the fruit it bears or from its practical consequences. These consequences reach far beyond what we now call the social environment: they concern the whole concrete reality that human beings nourish out of their own substance, beyond the limits of this life—the reality that constitutes their spiritual world.

This conviction has guided the author in constructing the work presented here in seven books. It is the fruit of more than twenty years of research in Iran itself, conducted in libraries and among close Iranian friends, together with years of teaching in Paris and Tehran. The method is essentially phenomenological, though it belongs to no particular school of phenomenology. Its aim is to encounter religious experience by allowing what is experienced in religion to show itself as it shows itself to those who experience it.
Hence the essential subtitle of this work: Spiritual and Philosophical Aspects. To speak of an “aspect” is to imply someone who sees it.

Yet here the observer—the phenomenologist—must become a spiritual guest of those to whom the religious reality appears, sharing with them the responsibility of bearing witness to it. Historical interpretation must therefore remain within the horizons of that reality rather than impose upon it some external framework, dialectical or otherwise. Only on this condition can the connections that the author repeatedly draws across different periods be understood as simultaneous expressions of the same underlying reality.
The first two volumes contain Books I and II of the work.

Book I brings to light several essential features of Twelver Shiism, or Imamism, which had deep roots in Iran from the beginning and became the official religion in the sixteenth century. These features are explored through what the author has elsewhere called the “phenomenon of the Revealed Book,” as it appears to those whom the Quran calls Ahl al-Kitâb, the “People of the Book”: the community embracing Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. In every branch of the Abrahamic tradition, interpreters of the Bible and the Quran have faced the same problems and tasks.

Each has sought to discover the Book’s true meaning. On both sides, the search for that truth—the spiritual meaning concealed beneath the literal wording—has led to similar methods for revealing the esoteric, or inner, meaning of divine revelation. The “phenomenon of the Book” lies at the origin of hermeneutics, the art of understanding and interpreting meaning. It seems likely that philosophers so preoccupied today with hermeneutics still have much to learn from the esoteric interpreters of the Bible and the Quran.

The technical term for the inner interpretation of the Quran is ta’wîl: literally, to “lead something back” to its origin, its archetype. Shiite metaphysics is governed by two inseparable ideas. The first is that God, in the divine Essence, is unknowable, inaccessible, and beyond every name.

The second is that God becomes manifest in a pleroma—a complete spiritual order—of Fourteen beings of light, who appeared on earth as the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones”: the Prophet, his daughter Fâtima, and the Twelve Imams. The inner meaning that Shiite ta’wîl draws from the literal statements of the Quran concerns above all these Fourteen. It therefore reveals a distinctive Shiite understanding of prophecy—one that refuses to place the future entirely in the past.

Unlike majority Sunni Islam, in which humanity, after the mission of the final Prophet, has nothing further to await, Shiism keeps the future open. Even after the coming of the “Seal of the Prophets,” something remains to be awaited: the unveiling of the spiritual meaning of the revelations brought by the great prophets. That work of interpretation was entrusted to the holy Imams, whose teachings fill many volumes.

But the full understanding of that spiritual meaning will come only at the end of our aeon, or age, with the return and manifestation of the Twelfth Imam—the Imam now hidden from sight, the mystical center of this world.

This way of interpreting revelation also implies a particular experience of time, expressed in a division of sacred history into periods: the age of the prophets’ missions is followed by the age of spiritual initiation. Here Shiite thought about prophecy meets the aspirations of the Joachimite movement in the West, with its expectation of the reign of the Spirit. Strictly speaking, however, this division already belongs to metahistory: because it concerns the ultimate destiny of humanity, it breaks beyond the boundaries of ordinary history.

The doctrine of the Imams, no less than the interpretation of revelation, confronted Shiite thinkers with problems resembling those that Christian thinkers encountered in Christology. Yet Shiite thinkers generally sought solutions in a direction rejected by official Christian Christology. Perhaps this is how Shiite spiritual knowledge preserved itself from being secularized into a program of social messianism.

Shiite metaphysics and Shiite spirituality are inseparable: each forms the substance of the other. Too long a reliance on accounts of majority Sunni Islam led scholars to identify Sufism with spiritual Islam as such. In reality, Shiite spirituality extends beyond Sufism. There are certainly Shiite Sufi orders, and most Sufi orders trace their spiritual lineages back to one of the Imams.

But the Shiite seeker of inner knowledge is already, by that very fact, on the spiritual Path (tarîqat), without having to join a Sufi order. At the summit of a mystical Sinai, knowing the Imam as one’s personal guide leads to knowledge of oneself.

Book II is devoted entirely to another equally fundamental and distinctive feature of Iranian Islamic philosophy and spirituality, one that was closely joined from the outset to the Shiism of many Iranian thinkers. Its defining word is ishrâq: sunrise, the rising of the light, the dawn (aurora consurgens) and its “Orient.” The philosophy of Ishrâq, understood as a wisdom of Light, is therefore an “Oriental” wisdom, and its philosophers—the ishrâqîyûn—are “Oriental” philosophers in a spiritual and metaphysical sense of the word Orient. They are also frequently called the “Platonists,” in contrast to Islam’s Aristotelian, or Peripatetic, philosophers.

At the beginning of this tradition of the “Platonists of Persia” stands the extraordinary resolve of a brilliant young thinker from northwestern Iran: Shihâboddîn Yahyâ Sohrawardî, who died at thirty-six in Aleppo, Syria, a martyr to his cause, in 1191. His writings plainly state his purpose: to bring the wisdom of ancient Persia back to life, the philosophy of Light and Darkness; in a sense, to bring the Hellenized Magi home to Islamic Persia, using the very resources of spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl) that Islam had placed at his disposal.

Some three centuries before the great Byzantine philosopher Gemistos Plethon, this Iranian thinker brought together the names of Plato and Zarathustra, or Zoroaster, as heralds of a single “Oriental” tradition reaching back to Hermes, the father of the sages. Platonic Ideas were interpreted through Zoroastrian teachings about angels. This interpretation of being acknowledged a third world whose reality philosophies confined to abstract concepts had been unable to establish.

Between the intelligible world and the world of the senses lies the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world: an entirely real world, not the merely “imaginary” realm to which outward-looking philosophies reduce it. It needs a word of its own: imaginal. Sohrawardî knew that by establishing the reality of this “third world,” he was also establishing the objective reality of prophetic revelations, mystical visions, and the events of Revelation. This theme would remain alive throughout the centuries of Iranian thought.

It is characteristic of this metaphysics of Light that it identifies the primal Source of light with what Zoroastrian sacred wisdom calls Xvarnah, the “Light of Glory.” From that Source proceed the hierarchies of archangels, structured as a synthesis of Zoroastrian angelology and the heavenly hierarchies of the Neoplatonist Proclus. The symbol of Xvarnah opens up inexhaustible connections and echoes. In earlier studies, the author traced correspondences between its forms of manifestation and those of the Holy Grail in Western traditions.

Indeed, the Grail—the mystical cup that mirrors the world—already appears in the heroic epic of ancient Iran. It also appears in Sohrawardî’s work, where it represents the passage from heroic epic to mystical epic, a decisive development in Iran’s cultural history. That transition takes shape in a series of short initiatory tales, almost all written in Persian. Their wealth of symbols allows Sohrawardî to guide the reader toward the goal of the reader’s longing even more effectively than his great systematic treatises. The author gives special attention to two of these spiritual tales, one rooted in Iran’s mystical epic tradition, the other in the wider traditions of spiritual knowledge called gnosis.
Sohrawardî’s “Oriental” tradition has remained active in Iran down to the present day. It also exerted a strong influence in India during the religious reforms of Emperor Akbar.

Together, these first two books present two essential dimensions of Islamic spiritual knowledge, or gnosis, as shaped by the mind and spirit of Iranian Islam. At a time when recent discoveries have given new impetus to the study of ancient Gnosticism and Jewish mystical knowledge alike, these investigations are especially timely.

Book III is devoted entirely to Iranian Sufism, as revealed through the work of one of its greatest masters, Rûzbehân Baqlî Shîrâzî (1128–1209). He was a contemporary of Sohrawardî, the Shaykh al-Ishrâq, or Master of Illumination. Yet while Sohrawardî came from northern Iran, Rûzbehân belonged to the south, to Fârs—Persis, or Persia in the strict sense.

His writings and teachings are particularly revealing of the spirituality of Iranian Sufism, especially where it differs from traditional Christian asceticism. The phenomenon of the “unhappy consciousness,” a name familiar to us since Hegel, belongs specifically to the history of Christian consciousness—even if today that consciousness increasingly insists on being “present in the world,” ashamed of its unhappiness or hoping thereby to lessen it. Sufism, too, confronts an opposition that it must overcome, but not the same opposition that made, or has made, the Christian unhappy.

The Christian has been torn between sin and the grace that justifies, between belief and knowledge; more crudely, between “mysticism” and “sensuality”; more abstractly, between factual historical truth and inner truth, between the object of faith embodied in history and spiritual reality unconstrained by time, between the literal wording of revelation and its spiritual meaning. With the secularization of a post-Christian world, the old affliction has merely acquired new names. Sociology assumes the authority formerly held by theology, assisted by psychoanalysis. Instead of sin, people speak of guilt complexes and frustration.

The Sufi, on the other hand, is neither a sinner seeking justification, nor someone sick, nor someone frustrated. He feels no need to be “justified.” He is a stranger, an exile. What he longs for, like seekers of spiritual knowledge in every age and place, is to find himself at home again, and therefore to meet the guide who will show him the way home. For him, this is the meaning of prophecy: the religious Law (sharî’at) revealed by the Prophet opens an inner Path (tarîqat) leading to spiritual Truth (haqîqat).

When that truth is lived and realized personally, it makes the Sufi a free human being. Mystical experience does not oppose prophetic revelation; it fulfills it, because it brings its hidden truth to realization. Without that inner truth, only an abstract monotheism (tawhîd, the affirmation of divine oneness) remains. What overcomes that abstraction is the idea—or rather the lived experience—of theophany, the manifestation of the divine. The divine Essence cannot be known, but divine acts reveal its attributes through countless manifestations.

A theophany is not God becoming incarnate. To perceive a theophany is to recognize iltibâs, the double meaning of every manifested being: it both conceals and reveals the invisible. Without the awareness that makes such a vision possible, one remains in a world of duality and oppositions. The devout believer and the dogmatic theologian alike are then, at bottom, polytheists without knowing it.

This awareness cannot arise by turning away from what is visible and perceptible to the senses. The visible must first be recognized as a veil, then transformed into a mirror. Among all human experiences, one is especially capable of bringing about this transformation: human love for a beautiful being, in which the soul is shaken and carried beyond itself by a manifestation of the divine. Rûzbehân gave Sufism a decisive new orientation by distinguishing two paths.

There are devout ascetics for whom human love has played no part in the beginning of the spiritual journey. And there are those for whom human love is the beginning of divine love. For them, the two loves are written in one and the same book, the book of one and the same love; the task is to learn how to read it. Only these latter seekers, whom Rûzbehân represents so completely, truly deserve the name Faithful of Love, because of their kinship with Dante’s Fedeli d’amore.

On this very path, Rûzbehân was not afraid to appear as a malâmatî: one of those who, in order to conceal the purity of their inner countenance, sometimes deliberately behave in ways that invite public blame. In this respect he may be regarded as a forerunner of another famous man of Shiraz, the great poet Hâfez, whose collected poems Iranian Sufis have always known how to read as a reminder of the mystical life.

At a friend’s request, Rûzbehân wrote a “spiritual diary” that is an invaluable document in the mystical literature of any age; it calls to mind certain passages of Swedenborg’s Memorabilia. It records his visions and dreams from the age of fifteen onward. Here we discover that from childhood he possessed an exceptional emotional intensity and gift for visionary experience. At fifteen he left his home. A vision revealed to him his hidden rank in the mystical hierarchy. Then came an extraordinary succession of visions: angels and beings of beauty, flowering landscapes, glowing red dawns. All Rûzbehân’s books are written in an intensely personal language, vibrating with an almost uninterrupted ecstatic lyricism that can make them difficult to read.

Yet this autobiographical diary gives us the evidence of lived experience through which we can trace the stages and trials by which the unfolding of love leads, along the path of divine manifestations, toward the inner realization of divine oneness, or esoteric tawhîd.

The first trial is the trial of the Veil. Rûzbehân certainly stands within the great tradition of Sufism, but here he contributes a remarkable insight of his own, one that reaches a summit of both lived and speculative mysticism. The “Hidden Treasure” brought the world into being in order to be known, and to know itself in its creatures. Spirit is the primordial act through which the holy spirits—the eternal spiritual individualities of beings—subsist. Every atom of existence is, no doubt, an eye wholly absorbed in contemplating the Light from which it arose.

But the Divine Being then experiences jealousy toward itself. By making itself an object to itself, by revealing itself, it is no longer simply its own witness: it now has a witness outside itself, someone other than itself. This is the first Veil. The Divine Being therefore seeks to draw itself back into itself; it turns this Spirit away from contemplation of God and directs the creature toward contemplation of itself. This vision of oneself by oneself is the second Veil.

The trial of the Veil is the very meaning of Creation: the descent of the holy spirits into earthly existence has no other purpose than to bring them through that trial to victory. To pass through it, the mystic must discover that self-knowledge is the very gaze with which God contemplates himself, and that the mystic is the witness through whom God bears witness to himself. Then the veil becomes a mirror.

Yet to seek what lies beyond the Veil is, Rûzbehân says, to fall into the “madness of the inaccessible.” Since Creation, God has never looked upon any world other than himself; he regards such a world with horror. Those who attain the awareness of being witnesses are the eyes through which God still looks at the world and, by looking, still takes an interest in it. They may remain unknown to everyone, yet it is thanks to them that the world endures. These mystics do more than perform a social role: they fulfill a task of salvation on a cosmic scale.

Here Rûzbehân’s insight comes very close to that of Meister Eckhart. The gaze with which I know God is none other than the gaze with which God knows me. This is the secret of the divine visions through which Rûzbehân advances toward esoteric tawhîd.

That advance is made possible by the unfolding of love, for love alone discovers the identity of witness and witnessed, of the one who contemplates and the one contemplated. It fills an entire book in Persian, perhaps Rûzbehân’s masterpiece: The Jasmine of the Faithful of Love. “With the eyes of the heart I contemplated uncreated Beauty; with the eyes of the intellect I sought to understand the secret of the human Form.” Love reveals the secret of theophanies because a theophany is, in its essence, the appearance of the divine in beauty.

Our age, intent on “demythologizing” everything, has worked so hard to strip beauty of its sacred character that awe in the presence of beauty may now seem strange, even alien. For the Iranian Faithful of Love, by contrast, it is a fundamental experience. The same is true of Ibn ’Arabî, whose influence on Islamic spirituality lasted eight centuries and who stands among the greatest witnesses to this mystical religion of beauty as the supreme divine attribute.

Rûzbehân adopts the Neoplatonic teaching: “Even before the worlds existed, the Divine Being was itself love, the lover, and the beloved.” He immediately confronts the great question debated in Sufi circles from the beginning: is it right to speak of love in relation to God? Whom does the mystic love when speaking of loving God? The whole of The Jasmine answers these questions.

In a sequence of chapters, it explores the prophetic meaning of beauty, contemplating the Prophet of Islam as the prophet of a religion of beauty. Drawing on the full resources of Platonic inspiration, it also uncovers love’s source before the beginning of time, weaving together the great themes of the Eternal Witness and the Eternal Bride. Sohrawardî had already set us on this path of the transfiguration of Eros.

Here, too, love is not transferred from one object to another, from a human object to a divine one. The transformation takes place in the lover. This is why its supreme image is the pair Majnûn and Layla—the Tristan and Isolde of the Persian and Arabic mystical epics. At the height of his love, Majnûn becomes the “mirror of God.” It is God himself who, in the lover’s gaze upon the beloved, contemplates his own eternal face.

This is what it means to reach the vision of vision, the esoteric realization of unity in which there is no longer either I + I or I = I, but I × I = I. In the intoxication of a consciousness carried beyond itself, the mystic may then utter the famous, seemingly excessive declaration of al-Hallâj: Anâ’l-Haqq (“I am God”). The case of al-Hallâj preoccupied Rûzbehân all his life. Again and again he explained and defended this celebrated utterance, in which the divine seems to speak through the human being.

Indeed, it is to Rûzbehân that we owe the preservation of a work by al-Hallâj in his immense Commentary on the Paradoxes of the Sufis. The author previously edited its Persian text. It is a true compendium of the Sufism of Rûzbehân’s time.

Book IV returns to a question first raised in Book I: the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. Its four chapters examine the works of four important writers of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, though the second, unfortunately, remains anonymous.

I. The first chapter concerns Sayyed Haydar Âmolî (born 720/1320; died after 787/1385–86). His extensive writings, often cited by later authors, had until now remained unpublished. The author has recently edited two of his treatises, which together form a genuine compendium of Shiite philosophy; for many of the others, sadly, no manuscripts have yet been found. Haydar Âmolî was a man of the north. He spent the first half of his life in his native Tabarestan, a province now included in Mazandaran, on the southern shore of the Caspian Sea. The works available to us so far provide the material for a moving spiritual autobiography, one especially characteristic of an Iranian seeker.

Born into a distinguished Shiite family of Tabarestan, Sayyed Haydar studied, among other places, in Isfahan. Until the age of thirty he enjoyed a brilliant and privileged life. He even served as a minister to his ruler and was briefly caught up in the political turmoil of the period. Then he underwent a profound spiritual crisis. Abandoning every worldly ambition, he took to the roads as a “pilgrim of God,” wearing a Sufi’s threadbare cloak. He traveled to the holy Shiite sites in Iraq, where he spent the second half of his life producing a body of work of enormous scope.

That work marks a major moment in the development of Shiite philosophy and spirituality. By itself, it is enough to show that Shiite thought as such was not, as some modernists would have it, a political invention of the Safavid period. Above all, it helps answer the difficult question of the original relationship between Shiism and Sufism. On a matter so central to understanding Islamic spirituality, a scholar of religion prefers to let those concerned speak for themselves and to take their answers seriously. That is why the discussion in Book I already drew so extensively on Haydar Âmolî’s writings.

Haydar approaches this question directly, for it seems to have been particularly urgent for him and those around him. He answers as a thinker devoted to inner meaning: in his view, Shiism is essentially the esoteric dimension of Islam. A Shiite who confines religion to its outward forms therefore cuts away part of the holy Imams’ own teaching. Conversely, Sufis, by affirming the inner meaning of divine revelation, show themselves to be the “true Shiites.” Unfortunately, they have forgotten their origin and have themselves diminished their inner teaching by excluding the doctrine of the Imams.

Sayyed Haydar wants to end this situation once and for all. He rejects both the Shiites who denounce Sufism and the Sufis who denounce Shiism. He must therefore confront several groups at once: the legalist Sunnis, the Shiites who have forgotten the inner meaning of their faith, and the Sufis who have forgotten their origins and what they owe, at the deepest level, to Shiism. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî would confront a similar situation some two centuries later. It is a tragic predicament that spiritual seekers in all three branches of the Abrahamic tradition have had to face in their different ways.

In pursuing this confrontation, Sayyed Haydar speaks as a disciple of Ibn ’Arabî, whom he cites repeatedly. Much of his effort goes into describing the passage from the theological understanding of divine unity, or tawhîd, to which the prophets called humanity, to the understanding of unity at the level of being itself, taught by the “Friends of God” in the footsteps of the holy Imams. These pages show how readily Shiite Iranian thought could absorb Ibn ’Arabî’s sacred philosophy, because it recognized in it something already its own. Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs was even understood as participating in the phenomenon of the Holy Book, since its author was believed to have received heavenly inspiration for it from the Prophet.

Yet despite his devotion to Ibn ’Arabî’s thought and work, Haydar Âmolî disagrees with him on one point that cannot be compromised. For a Shiite, the very meaning of the doctrine of prophecy is at stake. With all Twelver Shiites, Haydar holds that the Seal of walâyat—the spiritual authority and inner meaning of prophecy—cannot itself be a prophet, namely Jesus, as Ibn ’Arabî maintained. That Seal is, and can only be, the Muhammadan Imamate: in the person of the First Imam as the Seal of universal walâyat, and in the person of the Twelfth Imam as the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat. The whole destiny of the Shiite understanding of sacred history hangs on this distinction, whose full significance Book VII will bring to light. Haydar Âmolî could make no concession here.

Like many of his fellow spiritual writers, Sayyed Haydar had a particular gift for visions in the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world. His visionary gift went hand in hand with a taste for diagrams. A diagram of a vision he contemplated in the night sky over Baghdad offers a striking image of the structure of the pleroma of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones.”

II. The second chapter examines a treatise from the same period. Unfortunately anonymous, it gives an extensive commentary on a famous hadith attributed to the Prophet: “The Quran has an outward meaning and an inward meaning; that inward meaning in turn has an inward meaning, and so on through seven depths of inner meaning.” In stating this golden rule of spiritual interpretation—the movement inward toward the meaning of Quranic revelation—the hadith takes us back to the “phenomenon of the Holy Book.” Book I explored that phenomenon at length as the foundation on which the very meaning and vocation of Shiism depend.

Seen from this perspective, the anonymous treatise stands between the great work of interpretation by Semnânî, discussed below, and that of Haydar Âmolî, who devoted six substantial volumes to the Shiite spiritual interpretation of the Quran. The treatise formulates its central problem in terms familiar to interpreters throughout the Abrahamic tradition: what relationship does a revealed text, spoken in a particular language at a particular moment, bear to the eternal truth it proclaims? How does the divine Word come to be expressed in human words?

An objection naturally arises. If the divine Word is eternal, and therefore the events it reveals are eternal, in what sense can they still be called events? Our anonymous author answers by proposing precisely the idea of an eternal event, for which “before” and “after” cannot be measured by the one-way, quantitative time of chronological history. If the phenomenon of the Book marks the divine Word’s entrance into time, its spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl) leads it back to a kind of time that does not belong to history. Here we see the interpretation of the Book at work: it compelled these thinkers to face, and to find a way beyond, the problem of historical time.

As for the seven depths of inner meaning, each is associated with a different name for the Book, drawn from the Quran itself. Every name marks a level of meaning, and each level corresponds to those whose capacity for understanding reaches that depth. Interpretation is thus inseparable from a philosophical understanding of the human being.
We shall encounter this essential connection twice more below. It is a defining feature of a spiritual tradition grounded in the Holy Book’s different levels of meaning and understanding.

III. The third chapter studies a work of spiritual interpretation by Sâ’inoddîn Ispahânî (830/1427), a writer who belonged to an entire family dynasty of Shiite thinkers and spiritual masters. The work interprets an especially enigmatic verse of the Quran: “The Hour drew near, and the Moon was split” (54:1). The author offers something like a practical exercise in interpretation, beautifully illustrating the connection just described between our understanding of the human being and our interpretation of revelation: between ways of being and ways of understanding, between levels of understanding and the individuals capable of them.

By interpreting this verse at different levels of meaning, he sketches a religious typology embracing all the forms of consciousness then represented in Islam. As the penetration of inner meaning deepens, we encounter in succession the jurists and traditionalists (specialists in hadith), the theologian-philosophers of Islam (here, the scholastics of kalâm), the Aristotelian philosophers, the ishrâqîyûn or Platonists who continued Sohrawardî’s teaching, the Sufis, the Horoufîs, and the Shiites.

The author himself once again confronts us with an important question: can a genuine understanding of prophecy, or a genuine Sufism, exist without the Shiite doctrine of the Imams? The philosophical ideas are presented in a way that suggests an understanding of the Imams that dares not—or dares no longer—to speak its own name. This is one of the dramatic features of the history of Shiite thought.

IV. The fourth and final chapter concerns the writings and teaching of one of the greatest masters of Iranian spirituality, ’Alaoddawleh Semnânî (736/1336). By a paradox that is sadly far from unique, all his writings, in Persian and Arabic, still remain in manuscript. He belonged to the generation before Haydar Âmolî. Like Haydar, he underwent a profound spiritual crisis. Once a young page at the court of the Mongol ruler Arghun, he became a Sufi. His teaching follows the line of Najmoddîn Kobrâ (1221), the great master of Central Asian Sufism who was the first to pay close attention to the colored lights whose radiance appears to the mystic’s spiritual awareness.

Semnânî’s teaching is distinguished by an interpretation of the Quran that carries the inward transformation of its meanings to the furthest possible point. The relationship described above between interpretation and the understanding of the human being—between levels of meaning and levels of comprehension—takes on a remarkably original form here, combined with the theory of colored lights perceived in the mundus imaginalis.

At the same time, the succession of prophets, which in Islam recalls the early Judeo-Christian teaching of the Verus Propheta, or True Prophet, is also brought radically inward. This inward movement takes place through a physiology of the subtle organism concealed beneath the human physical body. There are seven centers or organs of this subtle physiology, each called a latîfa. They are not, to borrow Schiller’s expression, the “stars of your destiny,” but the “prophets of your being.” Each corresponds to a prophet, from the “Adam of your being,” through the “Abraham of your being,” to the “Muhammad of your being.”

Each latîfa has its own aura or colored light. Perceiving that radiance reveals to the mystic how far the subtle body has developed—that is, how far the body of resurrection has grown. Every Quranic teaching about a particular prophet must then be understood as referring to the corresponding subtle organ or center. In Sâ’inoddîn Ispahânî’s scheme, different levels of understanding were distributed among different groups of people. Here they have been brought wholly within the individual: the levels correspond to the subtle centers or organs of each spiritual seeker.

Above the seven latîfa, the “prophets of your being,” Semnânî repeatedly and mysteriously alludes to another, named after the Angel of knowledge and revelation: latîfa jabra’êlîya, the “angel Gabriel of your being.” At this summit of mystical understanding of the human person, we glimpse, once again, the secret of a doctrine of the Imams that dares not, or does not wish to, speak its own name.

Semnânî analyzes and describes in detail the cosmic forces and influences that constitute the seven latîfa. His is a magnificent vision, rich in inherited tradition yet unmistakably his own. Semnânî the mystic proves also to be a profound metaphysician, whose system invites many comparisons. His work therefore marks a major moment not only in Iran’s spiritual culture, but in the wider study of metaphysics and mysticism.

Book V celebrates the great flowering of thought that marked the Safavid Renaissance in Iran during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. This remarkable growth of philosophy, unmatched elsewhere in Islam, did not spring from nothing. Book IV traced some of what preceded it, while the Prologue explained how difficult this Renaissance makes our habitual divisions of the history of philosophy. Isfahan was then Iran’s great center of culture and the arts—though, unfortunately, that did not mean that its philosophers were spared difficulties. More than twenty thinkers and spiritual masters deserve mention as representatives of what the author has proposed calling the School of Isfahan. Only three, each outstanding in his own way, could be included here.

Indeed, the philosophers brought together under the name of this celebrated city differed greatly from one another. Iranian biographical and bibliographical dictionaries generally settle for too simple a division between “Peripatetics” (Mashshâ’ûn) and “Platonists” (Ishrâqîyûn). But the philosophers they call “Peripatetics” are not quite what we are accustomed to understand by that name.

MÎR DÂMÂD (1631) is a striking example. He was the intellectual master of several generations of Iranian philosophers. Much of his extensive work remains unpublished, later overshadowed by the writings of his most brilliant pupil, Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî. If Mîr Dâmâd is to be called a Peripatetic, we must remember that this “Peripatetic” left us not only substantial systematic treatises, several unfinished, but also ecstatic confessions, translated here. They are remarkable for two reasons.

First, they reveal the archetypal Images whose appearance in vision is always close to Shiite consciousness. Second, they show the Avicennian account of the universe bursting into an intensely dramatic vision. The narrative often recalls the account of ecstasy recorded by Plotinus in his Enneads, known to these Iranian philosophers through the work called the Theology of Aristotle.

Mollâ SADRÂ SHÎRÂZÎ (1640), Mîr Dâmâd’s most celebrated pupil, is by contrast a supreme representative of the “Platonists of Persia.” His immense body of work includes, among many other treatises, two great compendia. One is entitled The Four Spiritual Journeys. The other is a commentary on Kolaynî, widely used in Book I of the present work. Though unfortunately unfinished, it remains a monument of Shiite prophetic philosophy.

What first demands a philosopher’s attention in Mollâ Sadrâ is his metaphysics of being. It overturns the venerable metaphysics that gives priority to essence and replaces it with a metaphysics in which the very act of existing comes first. We may fairly speak of the continuing relevance of Mollâ Sadrâ’s concerns. This fundamental choice determines the distinctive positions of a thinker whose influence on Iranian philosophy has lasted to the present day.

Mollâ Sadrâ is the philosopher of metamorphoses and transubstantiations. His vision begins with the Soul’s descent to the depths of the abyss, followed by its ascent: reaching human form, it finally emerges at the threshold of the spiritual world, the Malakût. This is not an evolutionary theory, as some have too hastily suggested. It is a vision of a world rising through a divine action ceaselessly at work.

While affirming the transcendent unity of being, Mollâ Sadrâ’s metaphysics holds that being can be attributed to different things only by analogy, according to the varying degrees of intensity or diminution in the act of being that determines their essences. From this follows his principle of movement within substance itself, or “transsubstantial movement,” whose effects continue even into the human being’s existence after death. Mollâ Sadrâ understands matter in a way close to that of his contemporaries, the “Cambridge Platonists.”

In his thought, the boundaries between spirit and matter dissolve through the mediating reality of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world. Here he completes the metaphysics begun by Sohrawardî. He does so through his doctrine of Creative Imagination. This imagination is neither the work of memory nor a recombination of earlier sensory perceptions. It is an imagining Image: the original form in which the world first takes imaginative shape within us, and through which every soul creates its own paradise or hell.

By thus establishing the reality of imaginative experience independent of external perception, Mollâ Sadrâ anticipates modern inquiries, beginning with the work of Gaston Bachelard, that seek at last to establish a metaphysics of Imagination. For Mollâ Sadrâ, this Imagination is like the soul’s imperishable subtle body—the okhêma of Proclus. It shapes his philosophy of Resurrection and his vision of the human being’s threefold growth. For the philosopher, these processes of rebirth begin in this world, insofar as he becomes aware of the mystical implications of the act of Knowing.

Mollâ Sadrâ gives his own distinctive answer to the longstanding question of an essential union, without confusion of individual persons, between the soul and the Active Intelligence, which is the Holy Spirit. Understood in this way, the act of Knowing is fundamentally gnosis: saving knowledge that brings about a new birth. The name of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî should no longer be absent from our general histories of philosophy.

QÂZÎ SA’ÎD QOMMÎ (1691) also belongs to the School of Isfahan, but represents a very different direction within it. He studied under Rajab ’Alî Tabrîzî and thus came to profess a metaphysics of being unlike Mollâ Sadrâ’s.
